matched.set_a_axis: From self-sovereign heroic agency to repentant interdependence
matched.set_b_axis: From sovereign self-assertion to humble interdependence
matched.overlap_description: Both trace a movement from self-crowning chivalric agency and instrumental use of others toward dependence, repentance, and communal reconciliation.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-sealing enchantment logic to lucid disenchantment
matched.set_b_axis: From enchantment-sustained certainty to lucid self-renunciation
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Don Quixote's romance-saturated certitude, his enchantment-based rationalizations, and his final recovery of reason and rejection of knight-errantry.

matched.set_a_axis: From invented knight-errant to reconciled mortal self
matched.set_b_axis: From honor-seeking renown to repentant Christian humility
matched.overlap_description: These are a loose match: A emphasizes the invented chivalric identity and title accumulation, while B emphasizes honor, fame, and public renown. Both end in the rejection of the chivalric self in favor of a humble Christian mortal identity.

unique_to_a.axis: From honor-driven blame-shifting to merciful self-accountability

unique_to_b.axis: From euphoric-volatile self-righteousness to calm resignation

matched.set_a_axis: From instrumental command to affectionate reciprocal partnership
matched.set_b_axis: From instrumental patronage to grateful, affectionate partnership
matched.overlap_description: Both describe the Sancho relationship as moving from patronizing recruitment and instrumental command toward trust, esteem, emotional dependence, apology, and final blessing.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-authored ideal to anxious rescue fantasy and final relinquishment
matched.set_b_axis: From absolutized lady-fantasy to discarded chivalric illusion
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Dulcinea as a self-authored literary ideal that becomes an enchantment-rescue obsession and is finally abandoned when Don Quixote renounces the chivalric frame.

unique_to_a.axis: From impatient evasion to familial reconciliation

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From sovereign heroic self-assertion to humble interdependence
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A self-asserting, dominance-oriented fantasist who renames himself, invents Dulcinea, recruits Sancho through promises, imposes chivalric categories on reality, and treats other people chiefly as audience, instruments, or obstacles to his solitary heroic mission.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: A defeated, sane man who relinquishes heroic self-assertion, confesses his madness, apologizes to Sancho, rewards household servants, submits to God and the sacraments, and dies as Alonso Quixano among family, friends, and dependents, recognizing dependence and moral debt.

trajectory.position_description: Strongly agency-driven: he manufactures a knightly identity, names horse, self, and lady, reads the inn as a castle, demands dubbing, and enlists Sancho as an instrument and audience for his romance script.
key_moments: Loses his wits reading chivalry books and decides to become a knight-errant.
Names himself Don Quixote, his horse Rocinante, and invents Dulcinea as Lady of Thoughts.
Demands to be dubbed a knight and attacks carriers who disturb his armor.
Recruits Sancho with promises of an island governorship.

trajectory.position_description: Agency remains dominant but becomes hierarchical and coercive: he commands Sancho, punishes mockery, and explains every contradiction as enchantment. Dependence on Sancho grows, but communion remains patronizing rather than reciprocal.
key_moments: Charges windmills and converts failure into the Sage Freston's malice.
Frees galley slaves and demands their embassy to Dulcinea.
Performs the Sierra Morena penance and sends Sancho to Dulcinea.
Beats or threatens Sancho over Dulcinea and the lashes.
Is caged and carted home while interpreting captivity as enchantment.

trajectory.phase: Inflated public agency and staged performance
trajectory.position_description: His agency becomes theatrical and literary: he seeks fame, printed history, staged combats, and courtly recognition. He remains commanding, but increasingly depends on Sancho, hosts, and enchanters to sustain his role.
key_moments: Undertakes the third sally and defends chivalric truth.
Experiences El Toboso disillusion and the peasant-girl enchantment.
Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and confronts the lion.
Participates in Clavileño and the staged duenna adventures.

trajectory.position_description: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon strips him of active mastery. He accepts retirement, delegates judgment to Sancho, stops Sancho's whipping out of compassion, and returns home subdued and dependent.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and must retire for a year.
Endures pig stampede, mock resurrection, and ducal humiliations.
Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out in pain.
Admits his wits are confused and lets Sancho judge the peasants' dispute.

trajectory.position_description: He surrenders agency to Christian humility and communal obligation. He renounces knight-errantry, asks forgiveness, makes bequests, blesses Sancho, and dies lucid among others.
key_moments: Wakes sane and renounces books of chivalry as dark ignorance.
Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into mad knight-errantry and cancels his debts.
Calls his niece and housekeeper his daughters and provides for them in his will.
Dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The arc begins with a solitary hidalgo imposing a self-authored heroic identity on the world and commanding others as romance figures; it ends with a defeated, sane man acknowledging dependence on Sancho and his household, seeking forgiveness, and dying within ordinary Christian community.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-sealing enchantment logic to lucid disenchantment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Absolute conviction that chivalric romances are literal truth and that he is a knight-errant; inns are castles, windmills are giants, strangers are knights or enchanters, and every contradiction is the work of hostile enchanters rather than his own error.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Full lucidity: he admits his madness, calls chivalry books detestable absurdities, rejects the pastoral fantasy, renounces Don Quixote, confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies sane as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Reality is wholly assimilated to romance. His identity is unquestioned, and defeats are rationalized rather than doubted.
key_moments: Dubbing at the inn and armor-watching.
Mistakes windmills for giants and blames the sage Freston.
Frees galley slaves and interprets their ingratitude as villainy.
Treats the basin as Mambrino's helmet and rationalizes its appearance.

trajectory.position_description: He can say that he pictures Dulcinea as he wishes and chooses Amadis-style penance deliberately, yet this insight is absorbed into the chivalric frame. Contradictions become proof of hostile enchantment.
key_moments: Admits poets invent ladies and that he imagines Dulcinea.
Chooses Amadis-style penance as a deliberate performance.
Describes the cave of Montesinos vision and insists on its truth.
Sees a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea and blames enchanters.

trajectory.position_description: Staged courtly adventures validate him outwardly, but the false Second Part, the Knight of the Mirrors, and doubts about the cave vision increasingly destabilize his confidence.
key_moments: Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and explains Samson's face as an enchanter's transformation.
Hears the enchanted head and staged Merlin confirm Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Begins to doubt whether his cave vision was true.
Accepts Clavileño and Merlin literally despite earlier doubts.

trajectory.position_description: After the White Moon defeat he becomes more rational about ordinary matters such as inns and false histories, but still believes in enchantment, Sancho's penance, and omens. Delusion persists alongside genuine self-reproach.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and accepts a year's retirement.
Recognizes an inn as an inn and admits his wits are confused.
Reads the hare as an omen despite earlier condemning superstition.
Still hopes for Dulcinea's disenchantment.

trajectory.position_description: The delusion breaks completely. He recognizes his madness, repents, renounces knight-errantry, and frames his former heroism as dangerous illusion.
key_moments: Wakes from fever with his reason clear and calls chivalry books detestable absurdities.
Rejects the pastoral plan as nonsense and insists he is no longer Don Quixote.
Confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The novel tracks a long, non-linear consolidation of delusional certitude through repeated enchantment rationalizations, followed by late doubts under staged and real mirrors, then a final deathbed recovery of reason.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From chivalric self-myth and fame to humble mortal salvation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A modest hidalgo refashions himself as Don Quixote de la Mancha, accumulates chivalric titles, treats identity as a literary script to be proved by fame, and pursues eternal renown, honor, imperial rank, and public recognition through deeds dedicated to Dulcinea and posterity.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He rejects the Don Quixote identity as madness, insists he is Alonso Quixano, renounces chivalric glory, seeks confession, charity, fidelity, and forgiveness above fame, makes a sane Christian will, and dies as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Identity is invented through names and props: Don Quixote, Rocinante, Dulcinea, and the mock dubbing all confirm a new self. Renown is already the explicit goal.
key_moments: Takes the name Don Quixote de La Mancha after naming his horse and lady.
Believes the innkeeper's mock ceremony makes him a genuine knight.
Desires to become Emperor of Trebizond and win eternal name.
Demands the Toledo traders confess Dulcinea's beauty.

trajectory.position_description: Identity becomes increasingly public and literary: he adopts titles, treats printed history as proof of his reality, and makes honor legalistic and theatrical.
key_moments: Adopts the nickname Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
Renames himself Knight of the Lions after confronting the lion.
Defends fictional Queen Madasima with his life.
Rejoices that a printed history of his deeds exists and worries about reputation.

trajectory.position_description: His authentic identity is challenged by public performance, the false Second Part, and then shattered by the White Moon defeat. He begins to imagine a diminished pastoral alias, Quixotize.
key_moments: Seeks public vindication at Saragossa, in Barcelona, and before the duke and duchess.
Reads the false Second Part and resolves to disprove it by going to Barcelona.
Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and calls himself the most unfortunate knight.
Plans a pastoral retirement with the alias Quixotize.

trajectory.position_description: He rejects the pastoral alias and the entire knightly self. His final identity is the sane, penitent Alonso Quixano, and salvation replaces renown.
key_moments: Calls the pastoral plan nonsense and says he is no longer Don Quixote.
Insists he is Alonso Quixano, enemy of Amadis and all knight-errantry.
Makes a will and provides for his household.
Dies as Alonso Quixano the Good, with the curate testifying to his sanity.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The identity and honor arc moves from self-naming and title accumulation through public fame and counterfeit doubles to a final deathbed rejection of the invented knight in favor of the ordinary mortal name and Christian humility.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From honor-driven blame-shifting to merciful self-accountability
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Moral reasoning is mimetic chivalric honor: violence proves virtue, suffering confers honor, failures are enchanters' fault, and Sancho's body is instrumental to Dulcinea's cure.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He recognizes harm done to Sancho, stops the whipping when Sancho cries out, apologizes for drawing him into madness, cancels debts, seeks forgiveness, and makes amends in his will.

trajectory.position_description: He acts from romance scripts, rescues Andres, frees galley slaves, and attacks supposed villains, while rationalizing harmful outcomes as ingratitude or enchantment.
key_moments: Forces Juan Haldudo to promise payment to Andres, then leaves him vulnerable.
Frees the galley slaves and is beaten by them.
Blames Sancho for warning him about the galley slaves and for contradicting his fantasies.

trajectory.position_description: His devotion to Dulcinea and his honor justifies coercing Sancho and dismissing Sancho's judgment, though protectiveness and gratitude occasionally break through.
key_moments: Threatens to tie Sancho and whip him to disenchant Dulcinea.
Beats Sancho for disparaging Dulcinea.
Rescues Sancho during the boar hunt and defends him from the servants' prank.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat, he becomes more capable of restraint and dependence: he delegates judgment to Sancho and stops the penance when Sancho is in pain.
key_moments: Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out and covers him with his cloak.
Admits he is unfit to judge and lets Sancho settle the peasants' wager.
Praises Sancho as a great philosopher and accepts his counsel.

trajectory.position_description: He accepts responsibility for Sancho and his household, renounces the harmful books, apologizes, and seeks Christian forgiveness.
key_moments: Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into knight-errantry.
Cancels Sancho's debts and promises him rewards in his will.
Protects his niece from chivalry books and asks forgiveness of the false author.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Moral reasoning evolves from honor-driven violence and external blame toward mercy, restraint, and explicit accountability, culminating in the apology to Sancho and the penitent will.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From euphoric-volatile self-righteousness to calm resignation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He is emotionally volatile: euphoric in fantasy, anxious about chivalric procedure, furious when contradicted, physically violent toward Sancho and strangers, and prone to self-dramatizing despair or exaltation.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: In his final state he is calm, devout, tender, self-accusing, and resigned to death. The rage and theatrical self-pity are gone, replaced by sober repentance and affection.

trajectory.position_description: Mood swings rapidly from joy to anxiety to rage to self-pity. Violence and rhetoric are immediate responses to contradiction.
key_moments: Euphoria at being dubbed.
Rage at traders and carriers.
Beats Sancho over Dulcinea.
Fulling-mill humiliation and rage.

trajectory.phase: Righteous volatility under a chivalric code
trajectory.position_description: Anger is often legalistic and self-justifying, but he can also be serene and didactic. Mood remains reactive to honor, Dulcinea, and enchantment.
key_moments: Attacks Cardenio over a fictional queen.
Threatens violence during Micomicona adventures.
Delivers the serene Golden Age speech.
Remains stoic while caged.

trajectory.position_description: He oscillates between exultant performance and humiliation: lions, Clavileño, mock resurrection, and courtly mockery provoke grandiosity, alarm, and self-justification.
key_moments: Lion episode and renaming as Knight of the Lions.
Dulcinea enchantment despair.
Castle humiliations.
Mock resurrection and pressure on Sancho.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat his volatility cools into melancholy, self-reproach, and resignation. He still has flashes of irritation, but the dominant tone is weary acceptance.
key_moments: Broods over defeat.
Calls his wits confused.
Endures pig stampede and abduction.
Returns home subdued.

trajectory.position_description: Emotional life is integrated and quiet. He is repentant, grateful, affectionate, and ready for death.
key_moments: Wakes lucid after fever.
Confesses and makes his will.
Blesses Sancho.
Dies calmly.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Although stable delusion persists for most of the novel, the emotional register shifts from volatile self-righteousness to final resignation and calm.

relational_axes.axis_name: From instrumental command to affectionate reciprocal partnership
relational_axes.pole_start: Recruits Sancho with promises of an island and treats him as a subordinate, ignorant, cowardly, and a tool for witnessing and validating his madness; trust is high but esteem is low, and he punishes or threatens Sancho when contradicted.
relational_axes.pole_end: Depends on Sancho emotionally and practically, calls him friend and son, praises his natural wisdom, delegates judgment to him, stops his penance out of compassion, apologizes for leading him into madness, and rewards him in his will.

trajectory.position_description: The bond is hierarchical and transactional: Don Quixote promises rewards, ignores Sancho's warnings, treats him as an inferior witness, and punishes him when Sancho's mockery wounds his dignity.
key_moments: Persuades Sancho to become his squire with promises of an island.
Dismisses Sancho's warning about the windmills and about the friars.
Strikes Sancho after the fulling-mill humiliation.
Calls Sancho a fool and corrects his speech while relying on his reports.

trajectory.position_description: Conflict and dependence coexist: he beats or threatens Sancho over Dulcinea and the lashes, yet increasingly relies on his reports, care, and companionship.
key_moments: Sends Sancho to Dulcinea with the letter.
Beats Sancho for disparaging Dulcinea.
Refuses Sancho's demand for fixed wages and threatens to find another squire.
Reconciles tearfully with Sancho before the third sally and calls him friend and son.

trajectory.position_description: He recognizes Sancho's worth more often, calls him friend, grieves his absence during the governorship, and writes paternal counsel.
key_moments: Sends Sancho to El Toboso as his trusted intermediary to Dulcinea.
Warmly welcomes Sancho for the third sally.
Writes a paternal letter to Sancho as governor.
Praises Sancho's natural wisdom and defends him from mockery.

trajectory.position_description: The bond is tested by Sancho's governorship, separation, and return. Don Quixote writes affectionately, rescues Sancho from the pit, and values his counsel.
key_moments: Writes to Sancho as friend.
Rescues Sancho from the pit.
Leaves the castle with Sancho.
Accepts Sancho's truthful testimony over the garters.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat he becomes openly dependent and tender; he stops Sancho's whipping, values his judgment, apologizes for the whole knight-errantry venture, and provides for him.
key_moments: Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out in pain.
Delegates judgment to Sancho at the village wager.
Asks Sancho's forgiveness and cancels his debts in the final will.
Blesses Sancho, regrets leading him into madness, and wishes he could give him a kingdom.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The master-squire relationship moves from command and punishment toward trust, respect, emotional dependence, and final apology, making it the novel's central relational transformation.

relational_axes.axis_name: From self-authored ideal to anxious rescue fantasy and final relinquishment
relational_axes.pole_start: Constructs Aldonza as Dulcinea, Lady of Thoughts, the sovereign lady and judge of all deeds; devotion is literary, self-ornamental, and confirms his knightly identity rather than responding to a real relationship.
relational_axes.pole_end: The ideal becomes a persecuted enchanted lady whose rescue organizes his life; after his recovery of reason he renounces the chivalric frame that sustained her, abandoning the Dulcinea-enchantment quest and pastoral fantasy built around her, with no continuing relation to Aldonza depicted.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is invented to complete his knightly self: she is an abstract princess, judge, and motive for deeds, not a person he knows.
key_moments: Selects Aldonza Lorenzo and reinvents her as Dulcinea del Toboso.
Sends vanquished foes to her.
Invokes Dulcinea in combat, penance, and romance monologue.

trajectory.position_description: He admits he has rarely seen Aldonza and invents Dulcinea in imagination, yet still defends her supremacy with violence and devotional rhetoric.
key_moments: Tells Sancho that Dulcinea is really Aldonza but that he pictures her as an exalted princess.
Admits poets invent ladies and that he imagines Dulcinea.
Strikes Sancho for insulting Dulcinea.
Corrects Sancho's description of Dulcinea's eyes and mole to preserve her perfection.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea becomes the center of a disenchantment quest. After the El Toboso disillusion he insists she has been enchanted and treats Sancho's lashes as the necessary remedy.
key_moments: Sees a peasant girl on an ass as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Reports seeing the enchanted Dulcinea in the cave of Montesinos.
Vows to roam the earth until Dulcinea is disenchanted.
Accepts the staged Merlin's demand that Sancho whip himself for her release.

trajectory.position_description: Even after defeat, Dulcinea's disenchantment remains his central hope. He scans the road for her and ties his redemption to Sancho's fake lashes.
key_moments: Rejoices at the enchanted head's promise of Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Watches the road for Dulcinea after Sancho completes the lashes.
Counts the fake lashes on his rosary.
Sees omens that he will never see her.

trajectory.position_description: With the collapse of his chivalric identity, the enchantment project and pastoral fantasy around Dulcinea are discarded as part of his former illusion.
key_moments: Renounces books of chivalry.
Abandons knight-errantry and its Dulcinea project.
Dies as Alonso Quixano rather than as Dulcinea's knight.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea is the most intense object of Don Quixote's imaginative devotion, but the relationship is one-sided and literary; it intensifies into a rescue obsession and then fades as the chivalric worldview collapses.

relational_axes.axis_name: From impatient evasion to tender familial reconciliation
relational_axes.pole_start: He dismisses their warnings, secrets his plans, rebukes his niece for criticizing chivalry, and leaves home despite their distress, treating the household as an obstacle to his sallies.
relational_axes.pole_end: He calls them his daughters, reassures them, accepts their care in illness, protects his niece's inheritance from chivalry books in his will, and dies under their household care.

trajectory.position_description: The household is an obstacle to his sallies: he hides his plans, dismisses their fears, and treats their anti-chivalric concerns as ignorance or blasphemy.
key_moments: Accepts the housekeeper and niece's story of an enchanter taking his library.
Threatens his niece for calling chivalry histories fables.
Departs secretly or despite the niece's lamentation.

trajectory.position_description: Brief lucid conversation raises their hopes, but he reasserts knight-errantry and treats domestic opposition as a failure to understand his calling.
key_moments: Speaks so sensibly that the curate and barber hope he is cured.
Insists he will die a knight-errant.
Dismisses the housekeeper's threat to complain to the king.

trajectory.position_description: Weakened and finally sane, he becomes affectionate and dependent, addressing the women as daughters and accepting their care.
key_moments: Calls his niece and housekeeper his daughters and reassures them of his care.
Asks to be helped to bed because he does not feel well.
Makes a will protecting his niece's inheritance from chivalry books.
Dies under their household care.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The domestic relationship shifts from evasive rebellion against family concern to tender dependence and reconciliation in illness and death.
